pos: n. (an iron block on which metal is hammered into shape)
etymology: Old English anfilte, that on which a thing is beaten out, from an- (on) and a root meaning to strike. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Isaiah's mockery of the idol factory, where the anvil is the bed on which men beat out the god they will afterward pray to.
biblical_def: The anvil appears one time in Scripture, and it appears inside a satire. Isaiah is describing the assembly line of idolatry: carpenter encouraging goldsmith, one man smoothing with the hammer and cheering on the man who smote the anvil, the whole shop congratulating itself that the soldering is ready, and then fastening the finished deity down with nails so that it should not be moved. Every tool in the shop is a real tool doing real work. The iron is honest iron and the workmanship is honest workmanship; what is dishonest is the object. A god that must be nailed in place lest it topple is not a god, and Isaiah lets the tools tell us so without a word of direct argument. The anvil therefore belongs to the dictionary's doctrine of labour as much as to its doctrine of idols. God gave men hammers and anvils and the skill to use them, and that skill is a common grace. The question the anvil asks is not whether a man may beat iron, but what he intends to set up when the beating is done. The same forge that makes a plough makes a graven image, and the difference lies not in the iron but in the heart of the man at the bellows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an iron block with a smooth face, on which smiths hammer and shape their work; figuratively, whatever is beaten or wrought upon.
webster_full: ANVIL, n. An iron block with a smooth face, on which smiths hammer and shape their work.
ANVIL, n. Figuratively, any thing on which blows are laid; to be on the anvil, to be in a state of formation or preparation.
SMITH, n. One who works in metals; one who forges with the hammer.
FORGE, n. A furnace in which iron is heated and wrought; the place where anything is fashioned.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
scriptures: Isa 41:7

So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved.

The smith with the tongs both worketh in the coals, and fashioneth it with hammers, and worketh it with the strength of his arms: yea, he is hungry, and his strength faileth: he drinketh no water, and is faint.
The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold, and casteth silver chains.
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
corruption_summary: Craftsmanship is spoken of as if skill itself sanctified what skill produces, so that excellence in the making is treated as a warrant for the thing made; Isaiah's idol shop is excellent work in the service of a lie.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern celebration of craft as a nearly sacramental good runs straight into Isaiah 41:7. The shop in that verse is a good shop. The men encourage one another, the hammer work is fine, the soldering holds, the joints are true. Isaiah does not fault a single operation. He faults the product, and by faulting the product while praising nothing else he exposes the whole trade of self-made religion. Skill is a gift of God and remains a gift when it is bent; a forger's hand is often steadier than an honest man's. The dictionary therefore refuses the flattery that treats excellence as its own justification. Ask first what is on the anvil.

The second corruption is subtler and older: the assumption that a god men can secure is a god worth having. The workman fastens the image with nails that it should not be moved, and the whole logic of manageable religion is in that clause. The living God is the one who cannot be steadied, arranged, relocated, or improved, and men have always preferred the other kind. A faith adjusted until it sits quietly where it was set, offends no one, and never speaks back is an idol with better manners, and the nails are still in it.
roots_summary: Hebrew pa'am (H6471), a beat or stroke, rendered anvil in Isaiah 41:7; halam (H1986), to smite or hammer; charash (H2796), a craftsman.
roots_lines: Hebrew pa'am (H6471) — a stroke, a beat, a time; the struck block, and so the anvil of Isaiah 41:7.
Hebrew halam (H1986) — to smite, to hammer, to beat down; the verb of the man at the anvil.
Hebrew charash (H2796) — an engraver or artificer in wood, stone, or metal; the carpenter and the smith alike.
Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to refine or smelt; the goldsmith of the same verse, and the refiner of Malachi 3:3.
Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image; what came off the anvil in Isaiah's shop.
usage: “him that smote the anvil” — the one occurrence, inside a satire on idol-making.
“he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved” — a god that must be steadied.
The anvil as an emblem of honest labour that can be bent to dishonest ends.

pos: n. (a small knife for shaping a reed pen, and for cutting a written roll)
etymology: From pen and knife — the scribe's small blade, kept to trim the reed and scrape an error from the skin. The Authorized Version uses it once, and in that one place it is not mending a manuscript but destroying one.
biblical_def: Jeremiah dictated the word of the LORD to Baruch and sent the roll to be read in the king's house. Jehudi read three or four leaves at a time, and Jehoiakim cut the roll with the penknife and threw the pieces into the fire on the hearth until the whole roll was consumed. The detail that makes the account unbearable is the instrument. The penknife was the scribe's own tool, the blade that existed to serve the text, and the king turned it against the text. Nothing in the chapter suggests the king argued with the prophecy. He did not refute it; he shredded it, a few leaves at a time, with the patience of a man doing paperwork. The answer comes at once and without heat: take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned. The word was reissued, and the second roll carried additions against the king besides. The penknife is therefore the dictionary's emblem of every attempt to edit revelation with a private instrument, and of the plain futility of it. The fire on the hearth consumed the parchment and left the word untouched.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a small knife used for making and mending pens, and by extension any small pocket blade; in Scripture, the scribe's knife that Jehoiakim turned against the roll.
webster_full: PENKNIFE, n. A small knife used for making and mending pens.
ROLL, n. A writing formed into a cylinder by being rolled; a volume; a record.
SCRIBE, n. A writer; a notary; among the Jews, a writer and expounder of the law.
HEARTH, n. A pavement or floor of brick or stone on which a fire is made.
CONSUME, v.t. To destroy by separating the parts of a thing, as by fire; to waste away wholly.
scriptures: And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.
Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Mat 5:18
For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.
corruption_summary: Scripture is handled as material to be edited down to what the reader can accept, the hard leaves cut away and the remainder kept; Jehoiakim did this literally, and God simply reissued the roll with more against him in it.
corruption_paragraphs: The editorial knife has never gone out of use. It works now by canon within the canon, by declaring certain commands culturally bound, by preaching only the leaves that warm the hearth and never the leaves that indict the king. The method is gentler than Jehoiakim's and the result is the same roll, shorter. Jeremiah 36 is God's judgment on the method in advance: he did not debate the king, he dictated the roll again, and added many like words. Verbal plenary inspiration means the leaves the reader would cut are as much the word of God as the leaves he keeps, and the cutting hand has no authority over any of them.

There is a second and quieter corruption in that room, which is the flattery of the king's servants. Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll, and he would not hear them, and then nobody was afraid and nobody rent his garments. A word can be destroyed in the presence of men who know better and say nothing after the first objection. The dictionary counts that silence part of the sin of the chapter, and it is the part most easily repeated.
roots_summary: Hebrew ta'ar (H8593), a razor or scribe's knife; megillah (H4039), a roll or scroll; saphar (H5608), to write or number, whence sopher, a scribe.
roots_lines: Hebrew ta'ar (H8593) — a knife or razor; the penknife of Jeremiah 36:23.
Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll, a written volume; what the knife cut.
Hebrew sopher (H5608) — a scribe, a writer; Baruch's office at the dictation.
Hebrew qara' (H7167) — to tear or rend; used of cutting the roll, and of rending garments in repentance, which no one there did.
Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter; what survived the fire on the hearth.
usage: “he cut it with the penknife” — the scribe's tool turned against the scribe's work.
“Take thee again another roll” — the word reissued, and enlarged.
The penknife as a figure of editing revelation down to the acceptable.

pos: n. (the staff that holds the unspun wool or flax for spinning)
etymology: Old English distaef, from a root meaning a bunch of flax, and staef, a staff. It is the stick that carries the raw fibre while the spindle twists it into thread, and in the Authorized Version it appears once, in the hands of the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31.
biblical_def: She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff. The verse is one line in a long portrait, and it is easy to hurry past, but the Hebrew poem is deliberate about hands. This woman's hands seek wool and flax and work willingly; her hands hold the distaff; she stretcheth out her hand to the poor; the fruit of her hands is given her in the gates. Proverbs is not describing a hobby. Spinning was the foundation of every garment the household wore and of the fine linen she afterwards sold to the merchant, and the distaff is the homely end of a trade that clothed a family and turned a profit. Scripture honours this without a trace of condescension and without inflating it into a career. It sits between her provision for her household and her open hand to the needy, which is exactly where the Bible habitually places women's work: inside the home, ordered toward the household, and reaching outward from there with real economic weight. The last word of the chapter is not about thread at all. Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the staff from which flax or wool is drawn in spinning; used figuratively for the female sex and for women's domestic work.
webster_full: DISTAFF, n. The staff from which the flax is drawn in spinning.
DISTAFF, n. Figuratively, a woman, or the female sex; as the distaff side of a family.
SPINDLE, n. The pin used in spinning wheels for twisting the thread.
SPIN, v.t. To draw out and twist into threads, either by the hand or machinery.
FLAX, n. A plant whose fibrous bark is manufactured into linen cloth.
scriptures: She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff.
She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands.
Tit 2:5
To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
corruption_summary: Domestic labour is treated as a lesser life from which women must be liberated in order to matter, so that Proverbs 31 is read either as oppression or as sentiment; the text itself presents it as skilled, profitable, honoured work with the fear of the LORD at the centre.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors meet on this verse. The first is the modern reading in which the home is a cage and the distaff a symbol of confinement, so that a woman's worth must be established somewhere else before it can be established at all. Proverbs 31 will not support it: the woman buys a field, plants a vineyard, perceives that her merchandise is good, makes fine linen and sells it, and her own works praise her in the gates. That is not a diminished life. The second error runs the other way and sentimentalises the passage into a greeting card, all softness and no ledger, which flatters nobody and drops the flax and the profit and the strong arms out of the picture.

The dictionary holds the creational order the passage assumes. Titus 2 calls the younger women to be keepers at home, and Proverbs 31 shows what a keeper at home actually looked like with a distaff in her hands and merchandise in the market. Headship and submission are not idleness on either side. The passage ends where the argument must end, with the fear of the LORD, because a competent household without it is only a well-run vanity, and the verse says so plainly: favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain.
roots_summary: Hebrew kiyshowr (H3601), a distaff; pelek (H6418), a spindle or whirl; kaph (H3709), the palm or hand, the recurring word of the passage.
roots_lines: Hebrew kiyshowr (H3601) — a distaff; occurs only at Proverbs 31:19.
Hebrew pelek (H6418) — a whirl or spindle; also a district, from the turning.
Hebrew kaph (H3709) — the hollow hand, the palm; her hands hold the distaff.
Hebrew chephets (H2656) — delight, pleasure; she worketh willingly, with delight of her hands.
Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, ability, worth; the virtuous woman of verse 10 is a woman of chayil.
usage: “her hands hold the distaff” — the single occurrence, in the portrait of Proverbs 31.
“She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands” — the trade behind the thread.
The distaff as an old figure for the female line of a household.

pos: n. (a small spade or blade carried on the weapon, for digging)
etymology: From a root meaning a broad blade; in the Authorized Version not an oar but a soldier's digging tool, carried upon his weapon, commanded in the law of the camp in Deuteronomy 23.
biblical_def: Thou shalt have a paddle upon thy weapon, and when a man went aside to ease himself he was to dig with it and cover what came from him. It is the plainest sanitary regulation in the law and one of the most theological. The reason is given in the next verse and it is not hygiene: for the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee, and to give up thine enemies before thee; therefore shall thy camp be holy, that he see no unclean thing in thee, and turn away from thee. The presence of God in the camp reaches to the latrine. Israel's God is not a deity of the sanctuary only, ceremonially interested in the tabernacle and indifferent to the ground behind the tents. He walks in the midst, and the whole encampment is therefore ordered to his holiness, down to a blade strapped beside a sword. The paddle is the dictionary's standing answer to every division of life into sacred and secular compartments. A soldier burying his own filth in the dark was obeying God as truly as a priest at the altar, and for the same reason: the Holy One was present, and the camp was his.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a broad, short oar; also a small spade or blade for digging; in Scripture, the tool commanded upon the soldier's weapon in Deuteronomy 23.
webster_full: PADDLE, n. An oar, but more usually a broad short oar used without a rowlock.
PADDLE, n. A small spade or instrument for cleaning or digging.
CAMP, n. The ground on which an army pitch their tents; the army so encamped.
UNCLEAN, a. Foul; dirty; filthy; in the Mosaic law, ceremonially impure and forbidden.
HOLY, a. Set apart to a sacred use; pure in heart, temper or dispositions; free from sin.
scriptures: And thou shalt have a paddle upon thy weapon; and it shall be, when thou wilt ease thyself abroad, thou shalt dig therewith, and shalt turn back and cover that which cometh from thee:

For the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee, and to give up thine enemies before thee; therefore shall thy camp be holy: that he see no unclean thing in thee, and turn away from thee.

For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord:
corruption_summary: Holiness is confined to religious hours and religious rooms, with the ordinary and the bodily assumed to lie outside God's notice; the law of the paddle assumes the exact opposite and legislates for the ground behind the tents.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct that quarantines God into a sanctuary is ancient and comfortable, and Deuteronomy 23:13 offends it on purpose. If the LORD walks in the midst of the camp, there is no square foot of the camp he does not walk through, and the command about the paddle follows immediately and without embarrassment. Scripture is unembarrassed about bodies generally. It legislates about menstruation, emissions, skin disease, and the burial of dung, and it does so because a creation doctrine that stops at the neck is not the Bible's. The soldier obeys with a blade in the dark or he does not obey.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that general forgetfulness, and the principle to recover is the lordship of Christ over every sphere of life. The camp is holy because God is in it, not because the men in it feel religious. What follows is a doctrine of work, of sanitation, of soldiering, of the body, and finally of the church, which is now the camp in which he walks: follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.
roots_summary: Hebrew yathed (H3489), a peg, pin, or blade, rendered paddle; azen (H240), a weapon or implement; machaneh (H4264), a camp; qadowsh (H6918), holy.
roots_lines: Hebrew yathed (H3489) — a pin, peg, or blade; the paddle upon the weapon.
Hebrew azen (H240) — an implement or weapon; the gear a soldier carried.
Hebrew machaneh (H4264) — an encampment, a host; the camp God walks through.
Hebrew qadowsh (H6918) — sacred, set apart, holy; therefore shall thy camp be holy.
Hebrew 'ervah (H6172) — nakedness, an unclean thing; what God must not see in the camp.
usage: “thou shalt have a paddle upon thy weapon” — the single occurrence, in the law of the camp.
“the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp” — the reason given for the command.
The paddle as the standing rebuke to sacred-and-secular compartments.

pos: n. (a measuring rod or yard-stick used in trade)
etymology: From mete, to measure, and yard, a rod — the merchant's measuring stick. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the holiness code, where the measuring rod stands at the head of a list of trade instruments God claims for himself.
biblical_def: Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure. Four arenas are named and only the first is a courtroom. The other three are a shop. God legislates the length of the cloth merchant's stick, the honesty of the stones in his bag, and the capacity of the vessels he pours from, and he does it in the same breath as justice on the bench, because they are the same commandment. The verse that follows leaves nothing implied: just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt. Redemption is the ground of commercial honesty. A people bought out of slavery under a regime of forced quotas and short measures are not to run their own markets on the Egyptian model. The meteyard is a small thing, a stick, and Scripture treats a shaved inch on it as unrighteousness in the same word it uses for a corrupt verdict. Proverbs presses it further into the language of worship: a false balance is abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a yard, staff or rod used as a measure; in Scripture, the trader's measuring rod, which the law requires to be honest.
webster_full: METEYARD, n. A yard, staff or rod, used as a measure.
METE, v.t. To measure; to ascertain quantity, dimensions or capacity by a rule or standard.
MEASURE, n. That by which extent or dimension is ascertained; a standard of quantity.
BALANCE, n. A pair of scales; the instrument by which bodies are weighed.
ABOMINATION, n. That which is abominable; an object of extreme hatred; used in Scripture of what God detests.
scriptures: Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure.
Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt.
Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
Mic 6:11
Shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights?
corruption_summary: Business is treated as a morally separate zone governed by legality and market advantage rather than by God's law, so that a technically permissible short measure is counted shrewd; Leviticus puts the meteyard under the same word as a corrupt judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: The usual modern arrangement grants ethics jurisdiction over private life and leaves commerce to regulation. What is legal is permitted, what is undetected is profitable, and the conscience is engaged only where a statute reaches. Leviticus 19:35 refuses the division before it can be made. Unrighteousness in meteyard is unrighteousness, the same noun as unrighteousness in judgment, and God attaches his own name and the exodus to the demand. Micah presses the question that follows a man into his warehouse: shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights?

Proverbs supplies the register the dictionary keeps. A false balance is not merely unfair; it is abomination to the LORD, the vocabulary of idols and of the worst sins in the law. And a just weight is his delight, which is a startling thing to say about a lump of stone. It means the LORD takes personal pleasure in an accurate scale in a shop where no inspector will ever come. Honest measure is a form of worship, and short measure is a form of contempt for the God who brought them out of Egypt.
roots_summary: Hebrew middah (H4060), measure or extent, rendered meteyard; mishpat (H4941), judgment; mo'zen (H3976), balances; to'ebah (H8441), abomination.
roots_lines: Hebrew middah (H4060) — measurement, extent, a measuring rod; the meteyard of Leviticus 19:35.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice, a verdict; the first of the four arenas named.
Hebrew mo'zen (H3976) — a pair of scales, balances; just balances shall ye have.
Hebrew 'eyphah (H374) — an ephah, a dry measure of about a bushel; a just ephah.
Hebrew to'ebah (H8441) — an abomination, a thing detested; what a false balance is to the LORD.
usage: “in meteyard, in weight, or in measure” — the single occurrence, in the holiness code.
“A false balance is abomination to the LORD” — the shop under the law of worship.
The meteyard as the test of a man's religion where no inspector comes.

pos: n. pl. (barbed hooks for taking fish; in prophecy, the instruments of captivity)
etymology: From fish and hook. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, in Amos, where the women of Samaria are told they will be carried away with hooks and their posterity with fishhooks — the tackle of a fisherman applied to a deported people.
biblical_def: Amos has just called the women of Samaria kine of Bashan, fat cattle who oppress the poor and crush the needy and say to their masters, Bring, and let us drink. The sentence follows: the Lord GOD hath sworn by his holiness, that, lo, the days shall come upon you, that he will take you away with hooks, and your posterity with fishhooks. The image is the Assyrian practice of leading captives by hooks and rings, and it is chosen because it is undignified. Cattle are driven; fish are hauled. A people who lived for appetite are removed by the tackle used on appetites. Habakkuk uses the same picture of the conqueror who takes up all of them with the angle and catches them in his net and therefore rejoices and is glad, and Jeremiah has God himself sending for many fishers to fish them and many hunters to hunt them. The oath is what fixes the verse. The Lord GOD sware by his holiness, which is to say the judgment is not temper but character. And Amos ends the paragraph with the only counsel that fits: prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a hook for catching fish; in Scripture, the figure under which captives are led away, from the Assyrian practice of hooks and rings.
webster_full: FISHHOOK, n. A hook for catching fish.
HOOK, n. A piece of iron or other metal bent into a curve for catching, holding or sustaining anything.
ANGLE, n. A hook, or a hook with line and rod, for taking fish.
POSTERITY, n. Descendants; children, children's children, and so on indefinitely.
CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner, or of being in the power of an enemy.
scriptures: Amo 4:2
The Lord GOD hath sworn by his holiness, that, lo, the days shall come upon you, that he will take you away with hooks, and your posterity with fishhooks.
Hab 1:15
They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad.

Behold, I will send for many fishers, saith the LORD, and they shall fish them; and after will I send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the holes of the rocks.
Amo 4:12
Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.
corruption_summary: Divine judgment is recast as a regrettable natural consequence God permits rather than an act he swears to perform, which empties the oath of Amos 4:2 and with it the summons of Amos 4:12.
corruption_paragraphs: The common softening says that God does not judge, he merely allows sin to run its course, and that the prophets are describing political inevitability in vivid language. Amos closes that exit. The Lord GOD hath sworn by his holiness is the language of a personal, deliberate, covenanted act, and the verbs through the chapter are his: I have given you cleanness of teeth, I also have withholden the rain, I have sent among you the pestilence, I have overthrown some of you. Five times comes the refrain, yet have ye not returned unto me. Judgment here is not the absence of God from history; it is his presence in it, and the hooks are his tackle.

The second and more comfortable corruption is to read such a passage as belonging to other people. Amos is preaching to the prosperous and the religious, in a season of national success, to women at their cups and men at their sacrifices at Bethel. The chapter's last line is addressed to those who had every reason to think themselves safe, and it is the line the dictionary would put on the whole book: prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.
roots_summary: Hebrew ciyr duwgah (H5518, H1729), fish-hooks or thorns of fishing; tsinnah (H6793), a hook or barb; qodesh (H6944), holiness, by which the oath was sworn.
roots_lines: Hebrew duwgah (H1729) — fishing; with ciyr, the fish-hooks of Amos 4:2.
Hebrew ciyr (H5518) — a thorn, a hook, also a pot; the barb that takes the captive.
Hebrew tsinnah (H6793) — a hook or barb; the hooks of the same verse.
Hebrew qodesh (H6944) — apartness, holiness; the Lord GOD sware by his holiness.
Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, to return; yet have ye not returned unto me.
usage: “your posterity with fishhooks” — the single occurrence, in the sentence on Samaria.
“They take up all of them with the angle” — Habakkuk's conqueror with his tackle.
“prepare to meet thy God” — the counsel the passage ends in.

pos: n. pl. (hand-weapons; staves or javelins carried in the hand)
etymology: From hand and staves, the plural of staff — weapons held in the hand rather than thrown from an engine. The Authorized Version uses the word once, in Ezekiel's account of the burning of the weapons of Gog.
biblical_def: After the overthrow of Gog, they that dwell in the cities of Israel go forth and burn the weapons: the shields and the bucklers, the bows and the arrows, and the handstaves, and the spears, and they burn them with fire seven years. The inventory is deliberate. Ezekiel does not summarise; he lists the gear piece by piece as a quartermaster would, and the effect of the list is finality. Every category of weapon the invader brought is named and every one goes into the fire. The next verse presses the point into economics: they shall take no wood out of the field, neither cut down any out of the forests, for they shall burn the weapons with fire. The instruments of a great invasion become seven years of firewood, and the nation that was to be spoiled spoils those that spoiled them. Scripture's hope for the end of war is never disarmament by treaty. It is the LORD breaking the bow and cutting the spear in sunder and burning the chariot in the fire, and the beating of swords into plowshares happens when he shall judge among the nations, not before. Handstaves is a small word for that great settlement.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a staff borne in the hand, particularly as a weapon; in Scripture, among the arms of Gog burned by Israel for seven years.
webster_full: HANDSTAFF, n. A javelin, or staff borne in the hand.
STAFF, n. A stick carried in the hand for support or defence; a weapon.
BUCKLER, n. A kind of shield, or piece of defensive armour, worn on the left arm.
SPEAR, n. A long pointed weapon, used in war and hunting, by thrusting or throwing.
SPOIL, v.t. To plunder; to strip by violence; to take by force from an enemy.
scriptures: Eze 39:9

And they that dwell in the cities of Israel shall go forth, and shall set on fire and burn the weapons, both the shields and the bucklers, the bows and the arrows, and the handstaves, and the spears, and they shall burn them with fire seven years:

So that they shall take no wood out of the field, neither cut down any out of the forests; for they shall burn the weapons with fire: and they shall spoil those that spoiled them, and rob those that robbed them, saith the Lord GOD.
Isa 2:4

And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
Psa 46:9
He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire.
corruption_summary: Isaiah's swords into plowshares is quoted as a programme for human peacemaking with the judging Messiah cut out of the verse; in the text the disarmament follows the judgment and is its fruit.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 2:4 is probably the most misquoted verse in the political vocabulary, engraved on walls with its first clause removed. The verse opens with a judge: and he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people. Only then do they beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruninghooks, and only then do they learn war no more. The peace is real and it is coming, and it arrives by the rebuke of Christ and not by the goodwill of the parties. Psalm 46 says the same in the same order: he maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow. The bow does not lay itself down.

Ezekiel 39 fills in what that looks like on the ground, and it is neither sentimental nor abstract. Somebody has to gather the handstaves and burn them, and it takes seven years, and there is a further seven months of burying the dead in the valley. Scripture is sober about the cost of the settlement it promises. The dictionary declines both the utopianism that expects the plowshares without the Judge and the fatalism that expects the wars without the end of them.
roots_summary: Hebrew maqqel yad (H4731, H3027), a rod of the hand; neshek (H5402), weapons or armour; chaniyth (H2595), a spear.
roots_lines: Hebrew maqqel (H4731) — a rod, a staff, a stick; with yad, the handstaves of Ezekiel 39:9.
Hebrew yad (H3027) — a hand; the staff borne in it rather than cast from an engine.
Hebrew neshek (H5402) — military equipment, armour, weapons; what Israel burned.
Hebrew chaniyth (H2595) — a spear or lance; last in Ezekiel's inventory.
Hebrew shalal (H7997) — to plunder, to spoil; they shall spoil those that spoiled them.
usage: “the handstaves, and the spears” — the single occurrence, in the inventory of Gog's weapons.
“they shall burn them with fire seven years” — an invasion reduced to firewood.
“he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder” — who ends the wars.

pos: n. (a boiling vessel; one of four named cooking pots at the sanctuary)
etymology: From Old Norse ketill, a cauldron, itself from Latin catillus, a small bowl. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the indictment of Eli's sons, where the priest's servant thrust a fleshhook into pan, kettle, caldron, or pot and took whatever came up.
biblical_def: The law gave the priest a fixed portion of the peace offerings. Hophni and Phinehas replaced the law with a three-pronged fleshhook: the servant struck it into the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot, and all that the fleshhook brought up the priest took for himself. The four vessels are listed to show that no pot was safe and no rule applied. Worse followed, for they demanded raw flesh before the fat was burnt and threatened force if refused, so that the sin of the young men was very great before the LORD, for men abhorred the offering of the LORD. That is the deadliest clause in the chapter. Priestly greed did not merely rob God; it drove the people away from the sacrifice itself. God's own question to Eli names the offence exactly: wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice and at mine offering, which I have commanded in my habitation, and honourest thy sons above me. Malachi brings the same charge centuries later against priests who offered polluted bread and called the table of the LORD contemptible. The kettle is a small domestic word standing at the centre of the Bible's hardest warning about corrupt ministry.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a vessel of iron or other metal, used for heating and boiling water or other liquor; in Scripture, one of the four pots plundered by the sons of Eli.
webster_full: KETTLE, n. A vessel of iron or other metal, used for heating and boiling water or other liquor.
CALDRON, n. A large kettle or boiler, of copper or other metal.
FLESHHOOK, n. A hook to draw flesh from a pot or caldron.
OFFERING, n. That which is presented in divine service; an oblation; a sacrifice.
ABHOR, v.t. To hate extremely, or with contempt; to loathe, detest or abominate.
scriptures: And he struck it into the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot; all that the fleshhook brought up the priest took for himself. So they did in Shiloh unto all the Israelites that came thither.
Wherefore the sin of the young men was very great before the LORD: for men abhorred the offering of the LORD.

Wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice and at mine offering, which I have commanded in my habitation; and honourest thy sons above me, to make yourselves fat with the chiefest of all the offerings of Israel my people?
Mal 1:7
Ye offer polluted bread upon mine altar; and ye say, Wherein have we polluted thee? In that ye say, The table of the LORD is contemptible.
corruption_summary: Ministerial greed is treated as a private failing that leaves the ministry itself intact, when Scripture says the sin of Eli's sons made men abhor the offering of the LORD and brought the house down.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 2 will not allow the modern separation between a minister's conduct and his office. The fleshhook in the kettle is the whole scandal in miniature: a rule replaced by an appetite, at the altar, in front of the worshippers. And the consequence recorded is not chiefly that the priests grew fat but that men abhorred the offering of the LORD. Corrupt shepherds do their worst damage downstream, in the consciences of the people who watched. The office is not insulated from the man; it is exactly what the man's sin defiles.

Eli himself is the second warning, and the milder sin is the one the chapter dwells on longest. He rebuked his sons and did nothing, and God's charge against him is that he honoured his sons above God. A father's indulgence and a presbytery's reluctance are the same failure, and God treats the restraining that was never done as the cause of the judgment. The plurality of elders exists in part for this: so that a Hophni has somebody over him who will act, and an Eli is not the only one who can.
roots_summary: Hebrew duwd (H1731), a pot or kettle; kiyowr (H3595), a pan or basin; qalachath (H7037), a caldron; mazleg (H4207), a fleshhook.
roots_lines: Hebrew duwd (H1731) — a pot, kettle, or basket; the kettle of 1 Samuel 2:14.
Hebrew kiyowr (H3595) — a pan or laver; the first vessel in the list.
Hebrew qalachath (H7037) — a caldron; the third vessel in the list.
Hebrew mazleg (H4207) — a fleshhook of three teeth; the instrument of the theft.
Hebrew na'ats (H5006) — to spurn, to abhor, to contemn; men abhorred the offering of the LORD.
usage: “the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot” — the single occurrence, and no vessel exempt.
“men abhorred the offering of the LORD” — the damage done downstream.
“wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice” — God's own naming of the sin.

pos: v. (to fasten a door with a bar or bolt)
etymology: Old English bolt, a stout pin or bar. The Authorized Version uses the verb in the account of Amnon and Tamar, where a bolted door seals a crime already committed.
biblical_def: Amnon, having forced his sister, hated her with a hatred greater than the love wherewith he had loved her, and said to her, Arise, be gone. Then he called his servant that ministered unto him, and said, Put now this woman out from me, and bolt the door after her. The servant brought her out and bolted the door after her. The bolt is the last detail of the crime and the cruellest. It is not a defence; there is nothing left to defend against. It is the sound of a man shutting his sin outside and going back to his bed, and Scripture records the click of it because Scripture is honest about what men do. Tamar goes out crying, with ashes on her head and her garment of divers colours rent, and the narrative follows her and not him. The chapter that began with a bolted door ends with Absalom's knife two years later, and the house of David is never the same. A door can be bolted against a sister and it cannot be bolted against consequence. Solomon's counsel in Proverbs is the preventative the family never took: remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to fasten or secure with a bolt; the bolt itself being a strong pin or bar of iron used to fasten a door.
webster_full: BOLT, v.t. To fasten or secure with a bolt or iron pin.
BOLT, n. An arrow; a dart; also, a strong cylindrical pin of iron used to fasten a door.
LOCK, n. An instrument for fastening doors, chests and the like.
DOOR, n. An opening or passage into a house or other building, or into any room or apartment.
LUST, n. Longing desire; concupiscence; irregular indulgence of the appetites.
scriptures: Then he called his servant that ministered unto him, and said, Put now this woman out from me, and bolt the door after her.
And she had a garment of divers colours upon her: for with such robes were the king's daughters that were virgins apparelled. Then his servant brought her out, and bolted the door after her.
Son 5:5
I rose up to open to my beloved; and my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with sweet smelling myrrh, upon the handles of the lock.
Pro 5:8
Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house:
corruption_summary: Sexual sin is treated as a private transaction between consenting parties whose harm ends when the door closes; 2 Samuel 13 follows the bolt through two years to a murder and a rebellion, and tells the story from the victim's side.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's account of Amnon is unusually explicit about the anatomy of lust, and every stage of it contradicts the modern account. It begins as love in his own telling, becomes obsession that makes him lean and sick, is counselled by a friend who is wise in the world's sense, is executed by deceit, and collapses the instant it is gratified into a hatred greater than the love. Then the bolt. Nothing in that sequence resembles a private arrangement between equals, and nothing in it ends where the chapter ends. The dictionary names the act by its biblical name, which is folly and wickedness in Israel, and uses Tamar's own words for it: this evil in sending me away is greater than the other.

The second corruption is silence disguised as prudence. David heard of it and was very wroth and did nothing, being unwilling to cross his firstborn; Absalom said neither good nor bad to Amnon and waited two years with a knife. The passivity of the father and the private vengeance of the brother are both judged by the outcome. Where the law of God is not administered in a house, someone else eventually administers something else, and the bolt on that door was the beginning of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew na'al (H5274), to bar or bolt a door; deleth (H1817), a door; nebalah (H5039), folly or wickedness, the word Tamar uses.
roots_lines: Hebrew na'al (H5274) — to fasten, to bar, to bolt; the verb of 2 Samuel 13:17.
Hebrew deleth (H1817) — a door, a leaf of a gate; what was bolted after her.
Hebrew nebalah (H5039) — folly, disgraceful wickedness; no such thing ought to be done in Israel.
Hebrew sane' (H8130) — to hate; Amnon hated her exceedingly after the sin.
Hebrew 'ahab (H157) — to love; what he had called it before.
usage: “bolt the door after her” — the last detail of the crime.
“upon the handles of the lock” — the Song's door, opened in love rather than shut in shame.
“come not nigh the door of her house” — the counsel that would have prevented it.

pos: n. (a burning or burnt stick snatched from the fire)
etymology: Old English brand, a burning, from the root of burn. In the Authorized Version it is a stick already in the flames, and its one appearance is the LORD's answer to Satan concerning Joshua the high priest.
biblical_def: Joshua the high priest stood before the angel of the LORD, clothed in filthy garments, with Satan at his right hand to resist him. The LORD's answer is not a defence of Joshua's character: The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan; even the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire? Every word of the accusation is conceded. The man is filthy, the garments prove it, and no argument is offered that he deserves better. The ground of his acquittal is election and rescue, and the figure is a half-burnt stick pulled out of a fire by a hand that had no obligation to reach in. Then the order is given: Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment. That is justification in a sentence — the guilt removed and a righteousness given, neither of them the man's own. Amos uses the same image for a nation that would not learn from it, and Jude commands the church to do the plucking: others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a burning piece of wood, or a stick partly burnt, whether burning or after the fire is extinct.
webster_full: BRAND, n. A burning piece of wood; or a stick or piece of wood partly burnt, whether burning or after the fire is extinct.
BRAND, n. A mark made by burning with a hot iron; hence, a note of infamy; a stigma.
PLUCK, v.t. To pull with sudden force or effort; to pull off, out or from, with a twitch.
RAIMENT, n. Clothing in general; vestments; vesture; garments.
IMPUTE, v.t. To charge; to attribute; to set to the account of another.
scriptures: Zec 3:2
And the LORD said unto Satan, The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan; even the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?
Zec 3:4

And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment.
Amo 4:11
I have overthrown some of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD.
Jud 1:23
And others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh.
corruption_summary: Assurance is sought in the believer's improvement, so that a Christian who still sees filthy garments concludes he was never chosen; Zechariah 3 grounds the verdict entirely outside the man, in the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem.
corruption_paragraphs: The scene in Zechariah 3 is a courtroom, and the accuser's case is factually correct. Nothing turns on disproving it. The LORD rebukes Satan not by contradicting the evidence but by naming a prior act: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire? A stick already burning, pulled out by a hand that chose to reach. Where assurance is built on the believer's progress it will fail in exactly the season Joshua is in, standing in the filth and unable to argue. The Reformed answer is the text's answer. Election precedes and grounds the verdict; the change of raiment follows it and does not earn it.

The corruption running the other way is to read free grace as indifference to the garments. Zechariah will not have that either. The filthy garments are taken away, a fair mitre is set upon his head, and the very next words are a charge: if thou wilt walk in my ways, and if thou wilt keep my charge, then thou shalt also judge my house. Justification is immediate and complete; the walk that follows is commanded and real. And Amos is the sober footnote for any who take the rescue as licence — ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning, yet have ye not returned unto me.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'uwd (H181), a firebrand or poker, a stick snatched from the fire; ga'ar (H1605), to rebuke; bachar (H977), to choose.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'uwd (H181) — a firebrand, a stick used to stir a fire; the brand plucked out.
Hebrew natsal (H5337) — to snatch away, to deliver; the action behind the figure.
Hebrew ga'ar (H1605) — to rebuke, to chide; the LORD rebuke thee, O Satan.
Hebrew bachar (H977) — to choose, to elect; the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem.
Hebrew machalatsah (H4254) — a robe of state, change of raiment; what he was clothed with instead.
usage: “is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?” — the ground of the verdict.
“I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee” — the filthy garments removed.
“pulling them out of the fire” — the church commanded to do the same work.
